E0677.summary: In the author of Lucerna Salis, the gold of the Wise is not vulgar gold but a clear, pure water that becomes spiritual.
E0677.body: Atwood reports the author of *Lucerna Salis* as declaring “the gold of the Wise to be by no means vulgar gold; but it is a certain water clear and pure” [III.3 ¶32]. On the packet's reading, this water bears the Lord's lightning, from which all things receive life, and passes through the Alembic; hence, the quoted author says, “this is the reason, continues he, why our gold is become spiritual” [III.3 ¶32]. The gold of the Wise is thus identified with that water (QUOTED: the author of Lucerna Salis).

E0678.summary: In a Rosicrucian passage, Gold philosophical is named as the husband of Mercury; the text does not explain it further here.
E0678.body: In a passage attributed to the fraternity of the Rosy Cross, Mercury speaks: “my husband is Gold philosophical” [III.3 ¶64]. The text gives no further explanation at this point (QUOTED: fraternity of the Rosy Cross).

E0679.summary: The Golden Bough, the offering and talisman by which Aeneas descends; Atwood reads it as a ray of living light, the intellect, and a passport into hidden realms.
E0679.body:
Atwood treats the Golden Bough as what the Sybil sends Aeneas to find, “he may discover and bring to her the Golden Bough” [III.1 ¶15], and offers it as a parallel to the hidden object of the work. It is the required propitiation for the descent; literally part of the sacred equipage, “connected with the Mercurial caduceus” [II.3 ¶11], but read by Atwood ontologically as the intellect: “a ray of living light, golden and flexible, the true Brancha Spiritualis of Raymond Lully” [II.3 ¶11].

It is one of the “golden passports” into the hidden realms, and it is the bough, not the tree, that is to be taken, the small portion to start from: “Ramus, non arbor --- The bough, not the whole tree, is to be taken” [III.1 ¶32]. Atwood sets it beside other emblems: “Such was the Caduceus of Hermes --- the Golden Bough, the ferrying Cup of Hercules” [III.1 ¶36].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Aeneas passes Tartarus to Elysium “By propitiation, through the offering of the Golden Bough” [APP ¶168], which he is to “take as his talisman to pass through the Infernal Regions to Elysium” [APP ¶171]; there its tree appears identical with Proteus' last transformation [APP ¶171]. All voices are ATWOOD.

Asserted identities: = Brancha Spiritualis [II.3 ¶11]; = Caduceus of Hermes and ferrying Cup of Hercules (set in apposition) [III.1 ¶36].

E0680.summary: Something drawn to its native soil that passes through death and darkness, takes root, and blossoms into illuminating light; not explicitly identified.
E0680.body: Atwood (ATWOOD) describes the Golden Branch as drawn to its native soil, which “through death and darkness enters; and taking root at last, gathers strength to germinate and blossom, as a radiant flower” [II.4 ¶7]. The passage does not explicitly say what the branch is.

E0681.summary: In the Table Talk, the purplish outward appearance of the light of Life diffused over the seeker's body in the third life.
E0681.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood states: “The Golden Fleece is the outward appearance presented by the light of Life diffused over the body of the seeker in the third life” [APP ¶22]; the appearance is described as of a purplish luster (ATWOOD).

E0682.summary: In Basil, the one thing holding mercury, salt and sulphur, knowledge of which gives the root of life; called also a magnet.
E0682.body: Quoting Basil (QUOTED: Basil), the text presents the golden seed as the one thing that holds mercury, salt and sulphur; whoever knows it has the root of life. It is equated with a magnet: “this golden seed or magnet” [II.1 ¶11].

E0683.summary: The adept's water, found not in wells or depths but in higher places, as ripe Mercury rises.
E0683.body: Atwood quotes an adept: “Our golden water, says the adept, is not found in wells, nor in profundities, but in higher places” [III.3 ¶17]; the context connects this with ripe Mercury rising (QUOTED: the adept).

E0684.summary: Atwood's name for the central difficulty of the Hermetic Mystery: knowing the Salt and its solution.
E0684.body: Having treated the Salt and its solution, Atwood (ATWOOD) declares: “Here then liest the Gordian Knot of the Hermetic Mystery” [IV.1 ¶37]. The knot is thus the crux of the method: knowing the Salt and how it is dissolved.

E0685.summary: Cited as carrying the Christian doctrine of fulfillment, which Atwood adds to the other traditions as agreeing with them.
E0685.body: Atwood adds “the Christian doctrine of fulfillment” of the Gospel to the other traditions she has surveyed, as agreeing with them in the same tradition [IV.4 ¶28].

forms: Gospel tradition of the Life of Christ
E0686.summary: The Gospel account of Christ's life, to which, Atwood says, the Adepts compare the phenomena of their work and human redemption.
E0686.body: Atwood notes that the Adepts compare the phenomena of their work to the Gospel tradition of the Life of Christ and to human redemption [IV.3 ¶27]; she cites it as illustration.

E0687.summary: The divine gift by which alone, according to Norton and Kelly, the Art is found and obtained, rather than by study or will.
E0687.body: Two quoted authorities make grace the condition of the science. Norton's *Ordinal* calls it “A singular grace and gift of the Almightye;” and says of the science, “But only by grace, she is holy in her kind.” [III.4 ¶10]; on the packet's reading, the student must be proved able to receive it, and it is needed to undo God's conjunctions (QUOTED: Norton’s Ordinal). Kelly likewise says the Art comes not by reading, sitting still, fancy or will: “But, as I said, by grace it is obtained:” [IV.1 ¶19]; it is to be sought (QUOTED: Kelly). The records do not show Atwood qualifying either view.

E0688.summary: The ancients' exact art of growing and subliming the Spirit to higher degrees of concentrated essentiality in successive vessels or forms.
E0688.body: Atwood (ATWOOD) speaks of “that exact art of grafting and transplanting which the ancients practiced” [III.1 ¶9]: the Spirit is grown and sublimed to a third, fourth and fifth degree of concentrated essentiality, in as many representative vessels or forms. The horticultural image apparently stands for the stepwise concentration of the Spirit in the method.

E0689.summary: In a passage from Stoboeus via Dr Warburton, the next initiation, which affects the mind as death does.
E0689.body: In a passage cited from Stoboeus through Dr Warburton (QUOTED: Stoboeus / Dr Warburton), the next initiation, “initiation into the Grand Mysteries” [II.3 ¶37], is said to affect the mind as death does.

E0690.summary: Adept reputed author of the Water Stone, said to be Boehme's friend; Atwood cites his eyewitness vessel account and endorses his Stone/Christ analogy.
E0690.body:
Atwood lists Grasseus as reputed author of the Water Stone and a personal friend of Boehme [I.1 ¶70]; the note gives titles *Das Wasser-Stein des Weissens*, *Arca Arcano* and *Lillium inter Spina* [I.1 n83]. As J. Grasseus, his *Water Stone of the Wise Men* is said to have been published with the *Aurora* [I.1 ¶64].

Called “an ancient and much esteemed Adeptus”, he supplies (*Theatr. Chem.* 6:294) an eyewitness account of a world in miniature in the vessel: “Within this fabric (i.e., the consecrated vessel), was a certain mass moving circularly” [III.2 ¶25, III.2 n26]. Atwood reads this as the whole Hermetic laboratory.

He is named among the Adepts who compare the work to the Christian Creed [IV.3 ¶27]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), under the spelling Grsaeus, his *Aquarium* supplies the analogy of the Stone with Christ the Head Corner Stone, which Atwood endorses as a “versimilitude” [APP ¶46].

E0691.summary: In the Table Talk, inwardly a vocal utterance carved into the understanding spirit; outwardly its weakened material form, common idolatry.
E0691.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood (ATWOOD) gives an inward meaning: “A graven image means a vocal utterance carved into the understanding spirit” [APP ¶100], one worshipped by the heart. Outwardly, its weakened material form is common idolatry.

E0692.summary: St Paul, cited from 1 Corinthians 15:37 to support the teaching that what is sown must die to be quickened and rise in better form.
E0692.body: Atwood cites the great Apostle (St Paul), 1 Corinthians 15:37 [III.1 n36], to support the principle that what is sown must die to be quickened and rises in a better form: “thou sowest not that body that shall be” [III.1 ¶30]. She uses the passage approvingly.

E0693.summary: The ancients' art, which, Atwood says, Bacon knew nothing of, together with its subject.
E0693.body: Atwood (ATWOOD) says of Bacon that “he knew nothing of their Great Art, or of its subject even, and naturally mistook their hidden ground” [I.2 ¶24].

E0694.summary: In the Table Talk, Wisdom, the Universal Will, which dissipates the impure sulphurs in the individual will.
E0694.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood (ATWOOD) glosses the expression herself: “The great Salt Sea (Wisdom, the Universal Will)” [APP ¶94]. It dissipates the impure sulphurs in the individual will. Asserted identities: = Wisdom; = Universal Will [APP ¶94].

E0695.summary: The secret of the art, mentioned in the accounts of Kelly, Dee and Philalethes; the text does not say what it is.
E0695.body: Atwood (ATWOOD) relates that “the secret of making of the Powder was confided to Kelly some years afterwards by a dying monk” [I.1 ¶67], and quotes Dee: “Master E. Kelly did open the great secret to me” [I.1 ¶67]. Philalethes is said to have possessed “the secret” when young [I.1 ¶73]. These passages do not say what the secret is.

E0696.summary: An authority cited within Proclus's passage on the soul's entry into the Adytum of Life.
E0696.body: The great theologist is cited within the Proclus passage on the soul's entry into the Adytum of Life [II.4 ¶29]; the text gives no further identification.

E0697.summary: The highest reality, unknown because concealed in this life; it becomes known in Identity when the soul concentrates herself.
E0697.body: Atwood (ATWOOD) speaks of those who “seek to prove Reality in the Great Unknown --- unknown, because concealed in this life” [II.4 ¶42]. According to the passage, it becomes known in Identity when the soul concentrates herself.

E0698.summary: The totality contained proportionally in every portion of existence; simple, and known by contact and intuition in self-knowledge.
E0698.body: Atwood (ATWOOD) holds “every portion of existence to be continent and comprehended proportionally of the Great Whole” [III.2 ¶45]. Being simple, “it is simple, and not so much therefore an object of reason as of contact and intuition” [III.2 ¶46]; it is reached in self-knowledge.

E0699.summary: Paired terms: man prepares the way of the Greater Good in the Lesser, and the Lesser is blessed by the Greater.
E0699.body: Atwood (ATWOOD) gives man's task as “to prepare the way of the Greater in the Lesser Good” [III.4 ¶20], adding that “the Lesser is blessed by the Greater” [III.4 ¶20].

E0700.summary: The higher grade of ancient initiation, alone promising assimilation and final contact with the first principle; its doctrine concerned the whole universe.
E0700.body: Atwood (ATWOOD) says assimilation and final contact with the first principle were promised “to those who were initiated in the Greater Mysteries only” [II.2 ¶5]. Citing Clemens Alexandrinus with approval: “The doctrine of the Greater Mysteries, says Clemens Alexandrinus, related to the whole universe” [II.2 ¶5]. Later she says the revelations she has gathered partly describe “the visions, and awful accompaniments which took place in the celebration of the Greater Mysteries” [II.3 ¶49].

E0701.summary: In the monk continuing Basil Valentine, two domains each with its Vulcan; the Lesser World's Vulcan amends what the Greater Orb's leaves crude.
E0701.body: The monk, continuing Basil Valentine (QUOTED: the monk), says: “Whatsoever the Vulcan in the Greater Orb leaves crude and perfects not, that in the Lesser World must be amended by a certain other Vulcan” [IV.1 ¶40]. Apparently the Lesser World's fire completes what the Greater Orb's leaves imperfect; the text does not gloss either domain further here.

E0702.summary: In a quoted adept, the world whose virgin womb, Earth without form and water, is where Ruach Elohim is made body.
E0702.body: A quoted adept (QUOTED: the mysterious adeptest) speaks of “the virgin womb of the greater world, viz., that Earth which is without form and water” [III.3 ¶50], where Ruach Elohim is made body; then “The Son, born into the light of the macrocosm” [III.3 ¶50]. The same passage uses “macrocosm”, but the text does not explicitly identify it with the greater world. Asserted identity: its virgin womb = Earth without form and water [III.3 ¶50].

E0703.summary: Greek fable of Midas, which Atwood reads in the Table Talk as the will starved in possession of the aurific life.
E0703.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood uses the Grecian fable of Midas to illustrate the will starved in possession of the aurific life [APP ¶159].

forms: Greek and Alexandrian Platonists; mystics of the middle ages; the enlightened Fathers of the Christian Church
enlightened Fathers of the Christian Church
E0704.summary: Groups of writers whose works, Atwood says, give much evidence that the Eleusinian rites differed widely from common report.
E0704.body: Atwood says the writings of the Greek and Alexandrian Platonists, the mystics of the middle ages and the enlightened Fathers of the Christian Church give much evidence that the Eleusinian rites differed widely from common report [II.4 ¶56]. She cites them in support.

E0705.summary: Cited to support that the subject is least valued and outwardly dead but alive within, and that preparation removes superfluities.
E0705.body: Atwood cites the Greek Aristhenes in support of her account of the subject: least valued and outwardly dead but alive within, with preparation removing its superfluities: “Take that which is least, and draw it by artifice into the true ferment of philosophers” [II.2 ¶26, II.2 n18].

forms: Greek Catholics' hymn for St John's day
E0706.summary: A hymn cited to illustrate the tradition that St John made gold and gems.
E0706.body: Atwood cites the Greek Catholics' hymn for St John's day to illustrate the tradition of St John making gold and gems: “Qui de virgis fecit aurum Gemmas de lapidibus” [I.1 ¶24, I.1 ¶25]. Translation (ours): Who made gold from rods, gems from stones.
